data.context: Since 2015, a financially motivated threat group known as FIN7 (also referred to as the Carbanak Group) has emerged from the shadows and has been highlighted in a number of different incidents (https://www.trustwave.com/Resources/SpiderLabsBlog/Operation-Grand-Mars--a-comprehensive-profile-ofCarbanak-activity-in-2016/17/).

evidence.quote: a financially motivated threat group known as FIN7 (also referred to as the Carbanak Group)

data.context: This is part one of a two-part blog series detailing the team's engagements with FIN7 throughout early 2017.

evidence.quote: ENGAGEMENTS WITH FIN7

data.context: Part one of this series focuses on the network command and control techniques used by the actors.

evidence.quote: network command and control techniques

data.context: Operational Patterns Gigamon ATR observed FIN7 using several types of communications to maintain a foothold in their target environment, rotating their infrastructure throughout the operation in order to stay one step ahead of response and remediation efforts.

evidence.quote: FIN7 using several types of communications

data.context: For their primary command and control (C2), FIN7 used Cobalt Strike's DNS C2 as their method of maintaining access inside target environments.

evidence.quote: used Cobalt Strike's DNS C2

data.context: During the incident, Gigamon ATR observed that the attackers were consistently active between 08:00 and 23:00 GMT, with peak activity at 17:00 GMT and with minimal activity outside of that window.

evidence.quote: with peak activity at 17:00 GMT and with minimal activity outside of that window.

data.context: Before concluding operations for the day, the adversary would set their callback times to one hour, and change the mode of their communications to use A resource records (instead of TXT records).

evidence.quote: use A resource records (instead of TXT records)

data.context: Cobalt Strike DNS C2 DNS C2 leverages malicious DNS TXT and A RRs (resource records) queries which traverse standard recursive DNS channels and terminate at an attacker's authoritative DNS server.

object.name: malicious DNS TXT and A RRs (resource records) queries

evidence.quote: leverages malicious DNS TXT and A RRs (resource records) queries

data.context: The traversal of standard DNS channels make this technique effective for highly controlled environments where restrictive firewall, web filter or proxy policies are enforced; for example, in point of sale (POS) networks in the retail and hospitality sector, as well as other high-security financial transaction environments.

evidence.quote: The traversal of standard DNS channels make this technique effective for highly controlled environments

data.context: DNS Root TLD DNS 10 DNS DNS DNS POS Systems ISP DNS Internal DNS Registrar DNS Attacker C2 Server (https://blog.gigamon.com/wpcontent/uploads/2020/06/7.10_Figure-2-Example-ofDNS-C2-Traffic.png) Figure 2: Example flow of DNS C2 traffic.

evidence.quote: Attacker C2 Server

data.context: The specific C2 capabilities of Cobalt Strike are outlined in various blogs (https://www.cobaltstrike.com/) on their website.

evidence.quote: various blogs (https://www.cobaltstrike.com/) on their website

data.context: In the observed operations, FIN7 used the default communication settings present in Cobalt Strike without modification.

evidence.quote: used the default communication settings present in Cobalt Strike

data.context: During execution, PowerShell would make iterative DNS TXT queries, which would return encrypted data to be concatenated and then executed in memory.

evidence.quote: PowerShell would make iterative DNS TXT queries

data.context: These queries followed a pattern matching: aaa.stage.[encryptedstage].MaliciousDomain.com, baa.stage.[encryptedstage].MaliciousDomain.com, caa.stage.[encryptedstage].MaliciousDomain.com Emerging Threats Pro (https://www.proofpoint.com/us/threatinsight/et-pro-ruleset) has a signature for this part of the Cobalt Strike DNS C2 chain (SID 2809850) that should provide basic alerting.

evidence.quote: has a signature for this part of the Cobalt Strike DNS C2 chain

data.context: [encryptedstage].MaliciousDomain.com pattern, Gigamon ATR was able to detect attacker movement in real time, prior to confirmed control of the victim host, enabling immediate analysis of the new activity.

evidence.quote: attacker movement in real time, prior to confirmed control of the victim host

evidence.quote: The DNS TXT record staging process for Cobalt Strike

data.context: After staging, the attacker would shift to the use of DNS A resource records.

evidence.quote: After staging, the attacker would shift to the use of DNS A resource records.

data.context: Lateral Spread and Network Exploration Throughout our engagements with FIN7, Gigamon ATR observed heavy use of compromised credentials, specifically domain administrator accounts, to move throughout the environment.

evidence.quote: compromised credentials

data.context: Notably, FIN7 would frequently use the psexec_psh (https://blog.cobaltstrike.com/2015/07/29/cobaltstrike-2-5-advanced-pivoting/) command within Cobalt Strike, which uses the RPC Service Controller protocol to create a service on a remote host with the binary path set to execute a malicious PowerShell command.

evidence.quote: Notably, FIN7 would frequently use the psexec_psh
